name: Accent training
lead: Accent training, also called accent reduction or modification, is structured study of a language's sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation so speakers can be understood more easily or sound closer to a target accent.[1] Speech-language pathologists, acting coaches and linguists offer it, and speech-language pathologists do not regard accents as disorders.[1]

Some linguists caution that changing an accent takes years of interaction with native speakers.[1] Research on listener adaptation finds that listeners tune to accents, with generalization depending on training conditions.[2] A study of 1,699 listeners found that reactions to accents depended on communication context.[3]

paras: Programs target difficult vowels and consonants, stress, rhythm, intonation, linking and speaking rate, and can last days to months.[1]

No studies found of accent training as an appearance intervention. Related laboratory research on listeners shows that perceptual adaptation to accented speech can be specific to an accent[2] and that musical hearing skills relate to learning second-language English vowels.[4]
A 2007 newspaper report noted rising accent-reduction classes among immigrants.[1] The same article notes that accent-related employment complaints reach the US EEOC each year.[1]

card.summary: Coaching to change or clarify an accent; linguists say it takes years, and its appearance value is unstudied.
card.note: Full accent change can take years.

quick.overview:
Accent training teaches the sounds and rhythms of a target accent, usually to improve clarity.

It is offered by speech coaches and linguists; listener research exists but not on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Practice of target vowels, consonants, stress and intonation with feedback.
quick.risks: No physical harms documented; some linguists warn about unrealistic expectations.
